hints: Remember what an ideal gas pretends, that particles have no volume and no attractions at all between them.
Compare the four gases for strength of intermolecular forces, especially polarity and hydrogen bonding in $\text{NH}_3$.
Pick the gas that is most easily liquefied by attractions, as strong attractions pull it furthest from ideal behaviour.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes a gas ideal**

An ideal gas is assumed to have point particles with zero volume and zero intermolecular forces.

Real gases deviate most when particles attract each other strongly or are large and polarisable:
$$pV = nRT \text{ (ideal, no attractions)}$$

**Compare attractions in the four gases**

$\text{H}_2$ and $\text{Ne}$ are tiny and non-polar with only very weak London forces, so they are almost ideal.

$\text{CO}_2$ is larger with more electrons, so it has stronger London forces, but it is non-polar with no hydrogen bonding.

**Spot the strongest deviation**

$\text{NH}_3$ is polar and can form hydrogen bonds between molecules, giving much stronger attractions.

Strong attractions mean it is much more easily liquefied at room conditions, so it deviates greatest from ideal behaviour.

options.A: $\text{CO}_2$ does deviate because it is relatively large with London forces, but it is non-polar and cannot hydrogen bond, so its deviation is smaller than for ammonia.
options.B: $\text{H}_2$ is very small and non-polar with extremely weak London forces. It is very close to ideal under room conditions, not the greatest deviation.
options.C: $\text{Ne}$ is a single noble gas atom with no polarity and only very weak London forces. It behaves almost ideally at room temperature and pressure.
options.D: $\text{NH}_3$ is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, giving strong intermolecular attractions. These attractions violate the ideal gas assumptions most, causing the greatest deviation.
